narrative.overview:
ARP is a calm instrument panel for teams that run long agent pipelines and ratify what the agents propose. It reads like a well-kept research report: ink on a black ground, titles and figures in one engineered sans, and every number traceable to the page it came from. One colour, amber, is reserved for one reason only: a person must act. When nothing waits on anyone, no amber appears.

The system is precise and quiet. Cards are flat panels set off by a hairline; Geist carries titles, figures, text and controls, Geist Mono carries IDs and state, and a serif appears only where text is quoted from a source. Density is high enough for tables of thousands of companies while staying legible on a projector. There is one theme: black. Every component reads its colours from the same tokens.
keyCharacteristics: Black ground, ink accent for controls, amber reserved for 'waiting on a person'.
Status colours (green / yellow / red / blue) describe runs and ratings, never the person-must-act state.
Cards are flat: a panel fill and a hairline, no shadow.
Geist for titles, figures and reading; Geist Mono for IDs, labels and state; a serif only for quoted source text.
Five signature elements carry the identity: the Pixel mark language, the needs-you shape, evidence paper, the Orb and the status rail.
The start page leads with the five workspaces; everything else is reached from them.
The Orb, a gold hologram, stands for the agents; it is the only place where colour is spectacle.

rules.name: The One Signal Rule
rules.body: Amber means one thing only: a person must act. Never use it for branding, decoration, hover, focus of a normal control, or "running". When nothing waits, no amber appears anywhere on the screen. The Orb's gold is not amber and is exempt (see The Orb Colour Rule). Keyboard focus is an accent outline. A proposed item's box is neutral; only its "Proposed" tag and the needs-you shape carry the signal, so a queue never turns into a wall of amber. The flagged vote that needs a second person takes the signal border.

rules.name: The Brand Colour Rule
rules.body: Brand orange (#ff6a2b) appears in two places only: the logo apex and the square of the landing caption. It never appears elsewhere in the interface, so it cannot be mistaken for the amber signal.

rules.name: The Orb Colour Rule
rules.body: The Orb is gold and morphs through ice, ember and mint. These four colours live only inside the Orb's canvas and its phase label. They carry no meaning: they are not status and not the signal. Nothing outside the Orb may use them, and the Orb never uses `--hi`.

rules.name: Provenance Is Not Status
rules.body: Where a number came from (live, synthetic sample, portfolio holdings, not built) is shown with neutral marks: filled, half, ring, dashed ring. Metric numbers are ink. Green, yellow and red stay for status.

rules.name: The Status Is Not The Signal Rule
rules.body: Status colours describe runs and ratings. Red marks a failed run and also a Low (L) rating on Transition Barriers; that second use is a deliberate, confirmed exception, because the matrix reads as a traffic light. It never marks something waiting on a person.

rules.name: Chart Colours
rules.body: Charts with categories use four slots, `--cat-1` to `--cat-4` (blue, magenta, gold, violet; `lib/palette.ts` explains the validation). They are neither status nor signal. Board diagrams colour up to four flowchart groups with `--cat-1`, `--cat-4`, `--cat-2`, then `--muted`, never gold or amber, because amber means a person must act.

rules.name: The Arcade Exception
rules.body: The hidden arcade games draw in their own neon palette. They sit outside the product and are the only place where neon is decoration.

rules.name: The Icon Accent Rule
rules.body: Each workspace drawing has exactly one element that can light up: in the signal colour (`--hi`) when the workspace waits on someone, in the running colour (`--run`) when it runs. Otherwise the whole drawing is a quiet wireframe. The lit element is out of place while lit (lifted or taller) and moves once, in 850ms, when the status changes. Nothing else in a drawing moves.

rules.name: The Serif Means Source Rule
rules.body: The serif is for text quoted from a source document (the evidence paper). Nothing else uses it.

rules.name: The Pixel Means Presence Rule
rules.body: Pixel type marks the three places where ARP presents itself: the landing headline, the greeting and a workspace's title. Never set running text, tables or controls in it.

rules.name: The Mono Means Data Rule
rules.body: Mono is for IDs, labels and state. Never set a sentence of prose in mono for a "technical" feel.

rules.name: The Flat Card Rule
rules.body: Cards and stat tiles take a hairline, never a shadow. Nothing inside a card takes a shadow. Never stack a card on a card. Glows are status light, not elevation: a start card or process panel that runs or waits, its figure area and the lit part of its drawing glow in the status colour. Nothing else glows.

dos: read every colour from the tokens (`var(--hi)`, `var(--accent)`, `var(--text)`, …); the theme depends on it.
use amber for exactly one meaning: a person must act (see The One Signal Rule).
give anything that waits on a person the needs-you shape as well as the colour.
keep text at 13px or larger and at ≥4.5:1 contrast.
set titles and figures in Geist, IDs and state in the mono face, and keep the serif for quoted source text.
let wide tables scroll inside their frame, with the edge shadow cue.
donts: use amber for anything that doesn't wait on a person: not branding, not "running", not hover.
use brand orange anywhere but the logo apex and the landing caption.
use the Orb's colours outside the Orb.
animate a drawing while its status is unchanged.
put shadows on cards, tables, wells or inputs, or stack cards.
round markers: dots, steps and segments are square.
use emoji as icons or status markers; draw icons in the shared stroke family. (The ✎ on "Proposed" is a text glyph, not an icon.)
hard-code colours or fonts in components (third-party editors included); follow the live theme.
fade disabled or switched-off items with opacity; mark them with the well fill or a dashed edge and keep text legible.
